st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts Harvey as a useful legal-AI platform while materially developing the cluster’s operating-model and adoption thesis. It identifies concrete conditions for sustained value—time to develop fluency, trusted-peer diffusion and exploratory practice—and reinforces that adoption must remain bounded by risk awareness, specialist support and human oversight. Its reported time savings support feasibility but do not establish causation, market-wide economics or durable vendor advantage.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that access and prompt volume alone do not establish value. Its time-saving evidence is explicitly limited by self-defined power-user categories and estimated benefits.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s augmentation framing: Harvey is described as an assistant used to manage heavy workloads, while adoption is driven by client and commercial pressure. Its qualitative testimony does not establish quantified productivity, staffing reductions or firm-wide employment effects, consistent with the cluster’s caution about broader outcomes.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s qualified account of operational value and uneven adoption: it distinguishes sophisticated power use from basic usage and offers an illustrative document-analysis workflow. Its time-saving figures and practitioner account are interested and non-representative, so they demonstrate plausible value rather than defensibility, reliable legal performance or durable leadership.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: RSGI supports selective, workflow-specific deployment: it prioritises purposeful use, appropriate use-case selection, user confidence and integration into wider legal workflows over raw usage. Its accounts of time savings and organisational benefits also fit the cluster’s task-level-gains thesis, though they are commissioned, informal interview evidence rather than independent performance evaluation.
qs: Tom Whittaker, director and head of AI (advisory) at law firm Burges Salmon, stressed the need to “use things with purpose.” The tool is subservient to the task.

“You need to know how to fit it within the wider workflow.”  Sometimes, this means not using AI at all; and, from a managerial perspective, it means not worrying about maximising the number of power users (or “super users,” as they are also known in other contexts at Burges Salmon).

kp.k: Commissioned interviews underpin the report’s interpretation
kp.d: Harvey commissioned RSGI’s research. Its latest tranche comprised informal interviews conducted in February 2026 with 17 power users and technology experts from more than 10 organisations in Europe and the US, spanning ages 24 to 62 and seniorities from trainee to managing partner. RSGI explicitly distinguishes its overall interpretation from interviewees’ words.
qs: For this latest tranche of research, RSGI interviewed 17
report represents RSGI’s interpretation of their words.

kp.k: Earlier research reports substantially greater power-user time savings
kp.d: The table attributed to Harvey/RSGI’s November 2025 study, “Defining the Impact of Legal AI”, reports monthly savings of 15.7 hours for average law-firm users versus 36.9 for power users, and 11.8 versus 28.3 hours for in-house users. The narrative reports some outliers saving up to 45% of monthly time on data-heavy matters. These are reported savings; the earlier research left participants to define power usage themselves.
qs: it left the definition of power

kp.k: Power usage increasingly means value rather than volume
kp.d: Interviewees distinguish frequent use from sophisticated, high-value use. Repsol’s Javi Díez Tomillo describes qualitative power users as potentially using Harvey less while producing better results or extending its applications. Ashurst Advance’s Sarah Chambers prioritises powerful use cases and confident users rather than usage counts. Participants also distinguish expert users from champions who influence adoption without necessarily being experts themselves.
qs: better quality, or they are pushing the frontier.

kp.k: Fluency expands work beyond basic questions and summaries
kp.d: Adecco’s Surangkana Kehlstadt reports that, among about 170 Harvey licencees, roughly 10 make more than 200 prompts monthly and one approaches 700; these users also employ features beyond the assistant. At dentsu, Andie Garford-Tull cites a company survey showing movement from drafting and summaries toward exploratory analysis, including implications of new regulations. Schoenherr’s Andrei Salajan interprets repeated voluntary use as a sign of value, rather than presenting a measured causal relationship.
qs: make more than 200 prompts per month

kp.k: Workflow fit matters more than universal expert status
kp.d: Burges Salmon’s Tom Whittaker argues that expertise means identifying appropriate use cases and integrating the tool into the wider workflow, sometimes choosing not to use AI. He recommends ensuring colleagues know when to call on a super user, suggesting one per team, rather than maximising the number of experts.
qs: If you focus on the number, you’re looking at it from the wrong end of the telescope
He suggested one per team as a sensible ratio.

kp.k: Junior learning and specialist analysis involve different uses
kp.d: Lewis Silkin trainee Amanda Julius uses Harvey for basic legal questions and administrative extraction, describing it as filling knowledge gaps. An anonymous restructuring associate, Mr A, regards basic questions as a small fraction of its potential and instead uses Vault for iterative interrogation of complex contracts and agreements during crisis matters. These are accounts of different applications, not evidence that AI replaces professional formation.

kp.d: Anonymous innovation leader Ms L describes a pyramid of task sophistication, with routine work at the bottom and nuanced client advice at the top. She associates power usage with moving beyond lower-level tasks and continually trying new applications. This pyramid describes legal tasks, not firm staffing or associate-to-partner leverage.

kp.k: Career relevance and client expectations motivate adoption
kp.d: Mr A presents adaptation as necessary to remain relevant early in his career. Anonymous technology analyst Mr S reports partner-led adoption driven by clients’ own AI use and commercial considerations. Hawcock frames AI as a disruptive force requiring organisational evolution; interviewees’ comments are motivations and expectations rather than demonstrated market displacement.
qs: They understand the commerciality of it.

kp.k: Workload relief supports in-house retention and responsiveness
kp.d: Ms L and Tomillo identify heavy workloads as adoption drivers. At dentsu, Garford-Tull calls Harvey a retention lever because routine review and analysis can crowd out strategic work. She links efficiency to improving the legal department’s internal reputation and reports plans for a shared Harvey workspace with external counsel that could increase value and curb outside-advice expenditure. Her proposed power-user threshold is 700 prompts monthly, reached by just under 20 per cent of company users.

kp.k: Practitioners report time savings and improved perspective
kp.d: Foley & Lardner’s Chanley Howell reports that many tasks now take one quarter of their previous time, with four or five hours reduced to one. Lewis Silkin’s Cliff Fluet estimates nearly 60 working days saved in 2025 and describes benefits to communication clarity and objectivity. Mr A uses suitable prompts to explore opposing perspectives and weaknesses in a client’s negotiating position. These are individual reports and estimates.
qs: The only thing you can’t be objective about is yourself
I try to use it to get a holistic picture

kp.k: Training requires protected time and practical experimentation
kp.d: Interviewees recommend investing time beyond introductory courses, interacting directly with the tool, and beginning with routine emails, directory submissions and cost updates before progressing. Tomillo reports that Repsol’s usage initially rose slowly for about two weeks and then increased sharply. Fluet advises natural-language prompting rather than treating it as programming, and suggests microphone input.
qs: Don’t try to get anything, just see
Just talk to it in natural language.

kp.k: Usage targets coexist with persuasion and licence reallocation
kp.d: Markel’s Bryan Dressler monitors usage and presses his eight-person team to increase it. Adecco includes both prompt growth and experimentation with Workflows and Playbooks in legal and compliance KPIs; underused licences may be reassigned because demand exceeds availability. Andreas Vosskamp nevertheless stresses persuasion alongside formal requirements.

kp.k: Peer credibility helps adoption in decentralised law firms
kp.d: Kelly Boyd argues that law firms’ distributed partner businesses make top-down targets less effective than in corporations, favouring word-of-mouth diffusion through teams and networks. Estrella LLC’s Alberto Estrella says compulsion alone will not deliver integration; approximately half of his firm’s 15 Harvey licencees are power users, including everyone in its corporate department. Mr S describes trusted lawyers’ endorsements as social proof and says his firm is mapping these influence patterns.

kp.d: Chambers emphasises curiosity and organisational permission to experiment. Ms L and Garford-Tull argue that lawyers’ training to have the right answer can make failure or uncertainty difficult to accept. Boyd speculates, using the DISC personality matrix, that lawyers’ tendency toward Conscientiousness may be less conducive to experimentation than Dominance; the report presents this as speculation rather than a personality finding.

kp.k: Legal experience can strengthen creative, risk-aware AI use
kp.d: The report argues that defining complex tasks and explaining them clearly are legal skills transferable to Harvey. Lewis Silkin’s Alex Bazin suggests that senior lawyers’ confidence and understanding of risk allow more creative use, potentially making them heavier users, while also recognising that AI fits associates’ day-to-day tasks.
qs: They are more confident in the work they’re doing
they can use the tool in more creative ways.

kp.k: Human oversight remains necessary despite growing capabilities
kp.d: Howell cautions that Harvey will neither do the lawyer’s job nor deliver complete accuracy. Mr S stresses uneven capabilities, with performance above human norms in some areas and far below in others, and the need to advise partners and clients on human oversight. The report distinguishes experimentation from risking clients’ high-stakes interests.
qs: It’s not going to do your job, or
Partners and clients still need to be advised
on where human oversight is needed.

kp.k: Rapid development rewards reassessment and client collaboration
kp.d: Several interviewees describe colleagues abandoning AI after disappointing early results, whereas power users return and experiment again. Mr A reports revisiting AI after initially dismissing it and finding Vault transformative. Hawcock identifies the central adoption problem as giving time-poor lawyers time to learn; Chambers proposes firm–client relationships that permit joint experimentation and a shift toward asking better questions.

kp.k: External reports frame scaling as a human-capital challenge
kp.d: Hawcock cites OpenAI’s December 2025 report predicting movement toward scaled enterprise use and Wharton’s 2025 adoption report suggesting a possible 2026 inflection point. Both emphasise training, organisational processes and depth of use. These are external claims used to contextualise the interviews, not findings established by RSGI’s legal-user sample.
qs: Enterprise AI now appears to be entering this phase.
People and processes are the new constraint
Those pulling ahead are aligning talent, training, and trust with their investments.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hawcock presents intensive, purposeful use of Harvey as a means of saving time, improving legal work and shifting attention toward more sophisticated advice; interviewees also describe commercial and career pressures to adopt AI.
pts.d: Drawing on the November 2025 Harvey/RSGI report, Hawcock reports monthly time savings of 36.9 hours for law-firm power users versus 15.7 for average users, and 28.3 hours for in-house power users versus 11.8 for average users. The report describes outliers saving up to 45% of monthly time on data-heavy matters. Chanley Howell reports that many tasks formerly taking four or five hours now take one; Cliff Fluet estimates nearly 60 working days saved in 2025. Beyond speed, Fluet describes clearer, more objective communications; anonymous restructuring associate Mr A describes analysing large document collections and testing weaknesses in negotiating positions. Anonymous innovation leader Ms L argues that sophisticated use enables lawyers to concentrate on nuanced advice rather than basic tasks. Andie Garford-Tull reports a dentsu survey in which increasing fluency accompanied movement from drafting and summaries to more complex regulatory analysis. She describes Harvey as a retention aid that frees in-house lawyers for strategic work, improves other departments’ perceptions of legal, and could reduce outside-advice expenditure through a planned shared workspace with external counsel. Hawcock frames AI adoption as necessary to professional and organisational relevance; Mr A expresses a personal need to adapt, while Mr S reports partners responding to clients’ own AI use. These are reported findings, experiences and expectations, not claims of demonstrated profession-wide replacement. Sarah Chambers and Tom Whittaker qualify the emphasis on intensive use: value depends on selecting appropriate tasks and integrating AI into workflows, rather than simply increasing prompt counts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of a vendor-commissioned earlier study, informal interviews with selected users and managers, internal organisational usage information, and practitioner estimates.
pts.d: Harvey commissioned both the earlier value research and this follow-up. The monthly savings figures are attributed to Harvey/RSGI’s November 2025 'Defining the Impact of Legal AI'. Hawcock explains that participants in that earlier research estimated the number of power users and their time savings, with no imposed definition of power usage. The follow-up draws on 17 interviewees from more than 10 organisations, including law firms and corporate legal teams in the US and Europe. Interviews were informal and conducted in February 2026; the methodology explicitly identifies the overall argument as RSGI’s interpretation. Howell’s task-speed comparison and Fluet’s annual savings are individual reported experiences or estimates. Organisational examples include Adecco’s roughly 170 Harvey licensees, of whom about 10 made more than 200 prompts monthly and one approached 700; dentsu’s internal fluency survey and its proposed 700-prompt power-user threshold, reached by just under 20% of users; and Estrella LLC’s approximately half of 15 licensees identified as power users. These examples support the source’s discussion of adoption and usage, but are not presented as controlled productivity tests or legal-quality benchmarks. The document also invokes OpenAI’s December 2025 enterprise report and Wharton’s 2025 adoption report as external context for the expectation of scaled adoption and the importance of training. Those expectations belong to those cited sources, rather than being independent findings of the interviews.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported benefits concern 2025–early 2026 use; further gains are conditional on training, experimentation, suitable workflows and human oversight, with no fixed forecast for profession-wide transformation.
pts.d: The time-savings comparison comes from November 2025, Fluet’s annual estimate concerns 2025, and the follow-up interviews took place in February 2026. The prospect of mainstream enterprise adoption during 2026 is presented through external reports and industry expectations, not as an established outcome. Interviewees repeatedly condition benefits on investing time in learning and sustained experimentation. Javi Díez Tomillo reports that usage at Repsol increased slowly for roughly two weeks after introduction and then rose sharply; this is an organisation-specific experience, not a general mastery deadline. Howell cautions that Harvey will neither do the lawyer’s job nor be completely accurate. Mr S describes uneven capabilities and a continuing need to advise partners and clients about human oversight. Whittaker says appropriate task selection may mean not using AI, and suggests access to a super user—perhaps one per team—rather than maximising their number. Chambers stresses that value is specific to the user’s work and that confidence is complicated by rapid product and model changes. Proposed adoption mechanisms include protected experimentation time, peer demonstrations, support from specialists and, in some organisations, usage targets or licence reallocation. Kelly Boyd and Alberto Estrella argue that law firms’ decentralised organisation makes peer influence and personally experienced usefulness particularly important. Garford-Tull’s shared workspace with outside counsel remains a plan with potential savings, rather than an achieved reduction in expenditure.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source concerns law-firm lawyers, corporate legal teams, their managers and clients, with different benefits and adoption needs across seniority and work type.
pts.d: Interviewees range in age from 24 to 62 and in seniority from trainee to managing partner, alongside technology and innovation specialists. Trainees such as Amanda Julius use Harvey to explore basic legal concepts and extract document information. Experienced practitioners describe technical document analysis, strategic questioning, communications support and more creative use informed by their understanding of risk. Alex Bazin suggests that partners’ confidence and experience can support such experimentation, while also noting AI’s suitability for associates’ everyday tasks. For law firms, the claimed effects include greater capacity, relevance to AI-using clients and more time for sophisticated advice; the source does not quantify effects on headcount, associate leverage or pricing. Ms L’s pyramid describes task sophistication, not a staffing structure. For in-house teams, the claimed effects include faster handling of high-volume contracts and regulatory work, more strategic capacity, improved internal reputation, retention benefits and possible reductions in external legal spending. Managers and technology specialists are assigned responsibilities for training, identifying valuable workflows, enabling peer diffusion and explaining oversight needs. Clients are potential beneficiaries of more timely and valuable work and possible partners in adoption experiments. The source does not make a specific access-to-justice claim or demonstrate benefits for underserved members of the public.
